steps.title: Who are you, and what may you do?
text: In lesson 4 the server proved itself to the client. Now the client proves itself to the server. A server needs this, because it must know who is asking before it does anything.
Two questions follow. First, who are you? That is authentication. Second, what may you do? That is permission. A server that answers only the first lets every logged-in user do everything.

The lab runs three phases in order: mutual TLS, a login, and then calls. A signature tells you who is calling only when someone enrolled the caller's public key ahead of time. The login and the calls run in the clear so you can see the token on the wire, and a real system sends them inside TLS.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

claims.text: A signature shows who calls only because the key was enrolled ahead of time. The lab runs mutual TLS, then a login, then calls. The login and calls run in the clear so the token shows on the wire; a real system sends them inside TLS.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, opening paragraph, check table (device enrolled) and Roles and capabilities, last paragraph (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: Phase 1: the server asks for a certificate
text: The first phase is mutual TLS. In lesson 4 only the server showed a certificate. Here the server also asks the client for one.
Watch the server's CertificateRequest. It means: show me a certificate before we go on. A server may ask for this, and it does not have to.

claims.text: A TLS server that authenticates with a certificate may optionally request a certificate from the client.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 4.3.2 (Certificate Request)

steps.title: The client shows its certificate
text: The client answers with its own certificate. It carries the name pump-reader-4 and a certificate key. This key is separate from the login key you meet in phase 2.
The server checks it the way the client checked the server's in lesson 4: does it lead to a trusted root, is it in date, and does its signature verify.
Anyone can copy a certificate, so the card alone proves nothing. The next step shows what does.

steps.title: The client proves it holds the key
text: The client signs the handshake so far with its private key and sends the signature in CertificateVerify. The server checks it against the public key on the certificate.
A valid signature shows that the sender holds the private key behind the certificate. A client must send this whenever it authenticates with a certificate.

claims.text: Clients must send a CertificateVerify message whenever they authenticate with a certificate, and it is explicit proof that the endpoint possesses the private key corresponding to its certificate.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 4.4.3 (Certificate Verify)

steps.title: No certificate, no entry
text: Try it: have the client answer the request with an empty certificate. The server refuses with alert number 116, certificate_required. The check is named certificate_required alert.
Alert 116 means the client sent no certificate. Do not mix it up with alert 42, which comes next. A server may also choose to carry on without client authentication. This one is set to require it.

claims.text: Alert certificate_required (116) is sent by servers when a client certificate is desired but none was provided by the client. If the client sends an empty Certificate message, the server may continue without client authentication or abort with certificate_required.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 4.4.2.4 (Receiving a Certificate Message) and section 6.2 (Error Alerts)

claims.text: In the lab the removed-certificate row ends with code TLS13_CERT_REQUIRED and alert 116 (certificate_required), and the lesson 10 row of the UX design lists certificate_required alert for this try-it.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, Mutual TLS section and attack table (main, commit 279e9a1); docs/ux-design.md, section 8, lesson 10 row

steps.title: A damaged certificate
text: A certificate that arrives but is corrupt gets a different alert: number 42, bad_certificate. The check is named bad_certificate alert.
Try it: flip one bit of the signature on the client's certificate. The server cannot verify it, and it refuses.

claims.text: Alert bad_certificate (42) means a certificate was corrupt or contained signatures that did not verify correctly.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 6.2 (Error Alerts)

steps.title: Phase 2: a key that stays on the device
text: Mutual TLS proved the client holds the certificate key. Now the client logs in to get a token for its calls. The login uses a second key, the device key, enrolled ahead of time. Nothing in this lab ties it to the certificate.
The device key is a pair: a private key that stays on the device, and a public key that anyone may see. Find the private key in the secrets panel under the client lane.
A signature with this key shows the signer holds it. It says nothing about who the signer is until someone has linked the public key to a person or a device.

claims.text: The client certificate holds a fixed key (KeyIds.ClientTlsEd25519). The login key is a different seed drawn for each run and enrolled by the lab. The call phase runs on another connection and reads no certificate.
claims.source: Jared's re-check of PR #20 (comment 6658016121): three seeds gave tlsKey 0a1626172713245c and three different loginKey values; src/NetSec.Core/Labs/Lesson10Auth.cs, lines 185-186 and 201

steps.title: Login names a subject and a key
text: To log in, the client tells the issuer two things: the subject it claims to be, and the public key it will sign with. The issuer is the part of the system that hands out tokens.
Nothing secret travels here. Anyone can claim any subject name, so the claim proves nothing yet.

steps.title: Is this key on record?
text: The issuer looks up the subject in its own records and checks that it holds this public key for it. The check is named device enrolled.
This step gives a signature its meaning. The issuer trusts the key because someone enrolled it earlier.
Try it: log in with a key nobody enrolled. The key can sign fine, and the issuer still refuses, because it never linked that key to the subject.

tryIt.label: Log in with a key nobody enrolled

claims.text: In SSH public key authentication, the server must check that the key is a valid authenticator for the user, and must check that the signature is valid.
claims.source: RFC 4252, section 7 (Public Key Authentication Method: publickey)

claims.text: In the lab the issuer refuses a login with a key it does not hold for the subject, with code DEVICE_NOT_ENROLLED.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, check table and Attacks, L10-unknown-device (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: The issuer sets a challenge
text: The issuer answers with a random challenge, a number used once. It keeps a copy of the challenge it sent. Find it in the issuer column of the secrets panel.
The challenge makes the proof fresh. Because the issuer remembers it, only a challenge it really sent can be answered.

steps.title: Sign the challenge
text: The client signs the challenge with its private key and sends the signature back. The issuer checks it with the enrolled public key. A valid signature shows the sender holds the private key of an enrolled device.
This is a passkey-shaped challenge. Real passkeys work this way. It is not WebAuthn: this lab has no browser, no authenticator device, and none of the web checks WebAuthn adds.
Try it: send the same signed response a second time, after it has earned a token. The issuer has seen this challenge, so the check named challenge already used fails.

tryIt.label: Send the signed response a second time

claims.text: Web Authentication (WebAuthn) is an API for creating and using public key credentials scoped to a Relying Party, with authenticators and a user agent. This lab implements a challenge-and-signature shape only.
claims.source: W3C Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials Level 2, Abstract

claims.text: In the lab the issuer rejects a second ChallengeResponse for the same challenge with code CHALLENGE_REPLAY.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, Attacks, L10-replay-challenge (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: The answer must match the question
text: A fresh signature is still not enough. The issuer also checks that the answer names the challenge it sent in this login. The check is named challenge issued.
Without that check, an attacker could sign a challenge of their own choosing, or one recorded from an earlier login, and the issuer would accept it.
Try it: sign a challenge the issuer never sent. The signature is fine, the check fails, and no token is issued.

tryIt.label: Sign a challenge the issuer never sent

claims.text: The issuer compares the answered challenge with the one this login issued and refuses an unissued one with code CHALLENGE_NOT_ISSUED.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, check table and Attacks, L10-unissued-challenge (main, commit 279e9a1); review of PR #20, Blocker 1

steps.title: A token in three parts
text: The issuer now hands the client a token. A token is a signed note that says who the client is and what it may do.

Look at the claims. Split the token at its two dots and you get a header, the claims, and a signature. The claims read in everyday words: who issued it, who it is for, the subject, a role of cashier, a capability to void a sale, and an expiry time.
The issuer signs the whole note. Anyone can read the claims, and nobody can change them without breaking the signature.

claims.text: A JWT is a set of claims carried in a signed JWS. In the compact form its three parts (header, payload, signature) are joined by dots, and the exp claim sets an expiration time.
claims.source: RFC 7515, section 7.1 (JWS Compact Serialization); RFC 7519, section 4.1.4 (exp Claim)

claims.text: The iss claim identifies who issued a JWT, the sub claim identifies its subject, and the aud claim identifies the recipients it is intended for.
claims.source: RFC 7519, sections 4.1.1 (iss), 4.1.2 (sub) and 4.1.3 (aud); docs/lesson-10-names.md, Roles and capabilities (the token holds iss, aud, sub, roles, cap, iat, exp, cnf.jkt)

steps.title: Phase 3: the server checks the token's signature
text: The client now makes a call: ReadTotals. It sends the token along. The server checks the issuer's signature on the token before it trusts any claim in it.
Try it: change one byte of the claims. The signature no longer fits, and the check named token signature fails.

tryIt.label: Change one byte of the token claims

steps.title: A token ends
text: A token carries an expiry time. The server refuses a token that has run out. The check is named token expiry.
Short lives limit the harm of a stolen token. A thief can use it only until it ends.
Try it: have the issuer write a token that has already expired. The check fails.

steps.title: A token is for one server
text: The token names the server it is meant for, in its audience claim. The server checks that the name is its own. The check is named token audience.
Without it, a token made for one service could be used at another service that trusts the same issuer.
Try it: have the issuer write the token for another server. The check fails.

tryIt.label: Use a token written for another server

claims.text: Each principal intended to process a JWT must identify itself with a value in the audience claim, and if it does not, the JWT must be rejected.
claims.source: RFC 7519, section 4.1.3 (aud Claim)

claims.text: In the lab the server refuses a token written for another server with code TOKEN_BAD_AUDIENCE.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, Attacks, L10-wrong-audience (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: A stolen token is not enough
text: Here is the weak spot. A token is just text. If a thief copies it, the server cannot tell the thief from the client.

So every call also carries a fresh proof. The proof is a short signed note made with the client's device key. It names the method, the address, a hash of the token, and a one-time id. This idea is called {{term:dpop}}.
Try it: use the token with a proof made by a different key. The proof binds the token to the client's key, so the check named proof binding fails.

tryIt.label: Use the token with another key's proof

claims.text: A DPoP proof is a JWT signed with a private key chosen by the client. It carries the public key in its header, and its claims include jti, htm (HTTP method), htu (target URI), iat (creation time), and, with an access token, ath (hash of the access token).
claims.source: RFC 9449, section 4.2 (DPoP Proof JWT Syntax)

claims.text: DPoP is a mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth 2.0 tokens via a proof-of-possession mechanism on the application level. The lab applies the same idea to its own token, not to OAuth.
claims.source: RFC 9449, Abstract; docs/lesson-10-names.md, check table, proof binding row (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: Each proof works once
text: A thief who records one call could send the same proof again. The server defends in two ways. It rejects proofs older than 60 seconds, which is the check named proof age. It also remembers each proof's one-time id.
A real server must keep those used ids for the whole 60-second window, or an old proof could slip back in. This lab keeps them for one run only.
The lab also issues no DPoP nonce. A server may add a nonce to shorten a proof's life, and RFC 9449 makes it optional.
Try it: send ReadTotals again with the same proof. The server has seen that id, so the check named jti already used fails.

claims.text: Servers must accept DPoP proofs only for a limited time after creation, and can store each proof's jti for that window to decline repeated use. A single-use check may not always be feasible when servers share no state.
claims.source: RFC 9449, section 11.1 (DPoP Proof Replay)

claims.text: The lab accepts a proof whose iat is within 60 seconds, and it keeps the used proof ids for one run only. It issues no DPoP nonce.
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, check table (proof age; no nonce check is listed) (main, commit 279e9a1); src/NetSec.Core/Labs/Lesson10Auth.cs, Session._seen (a per-session dictionary of used challenges and proof ids)

claims.text: An authorization server may supply a nonce to be included in the DPoP proof to limit the lifetime of proofs; the mechanism is optional.
claims.source: RFC 9449, section 8 (Authorization Server-Provided Nonce)

steps.title: Who you are is not what you may do
text: By now the server has checked the token and the proof. The calls run on their own connection, and the server reads no certificate there. It knows the call came from a holder of an enrolled key and a token the issuer signed. It still must decide whether this caller may do this action. That is the permission check.
A role is a job title. The role cashier may read totals. A capability is a single right. The capability void-sale lets the holder void a sale, and the token carries it by name.
Try it: call Refund. The token has the role cashier and the capability void-sale, but it has no refund capability. The check named permission check fails.

claims.text: In the lab, read-totals needs the role cashier or manager; void-sale and refund each need a capability of that name. The normal token holds roles [cashier] and cap [void-sale].
claims.source: docs/lesson-10-names.md, Roles and capabilities (main, commit 279e9a1)

steps.title: Three ways a client proves itself
text: You have now seen three ways to prove who a client is: a certificate in TLS (mutual TLS), a signed challenge, and a token with a proof.
Each one rests on a key or certificate the server trusts ahead of time. A signature on its own proves only that the signer holds a key. The enrolment turns that into who.
Remember the setting. The login and calls here run in the clear so you can read them. A real system sends them inside TLS.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.
